paras: The attempted lynching of Pat Carmody was a Saturday-night armed attack, most likely on September 23, 1882, on the house of P. (Pat) Carmody near San Marcial, New Mexico Territory, by people who suspected him of leading the mob that had hanged Wm. Wiggins the night before. Carmody held his fortified house through an exchange of some two hundred shots and later took refuge with soldiers at Fort Craig.

According to a Socorro dispatch dated September 29, Wm. Wiggins was taken from his house at San Marcial on a Friday night and hanged over his own door in sight of his wife and children. The dispatch said he had been the main witness in a peon case and was hanged "to save a few from just punishment." An Albuquerque correspondent described Wiggins as an old soldier of the Florida and Mexican wars who had come to the region in 1846.

On the following Saturday night, the dispatch reported, "a number of people" concluded that Carmody, whom it called "a renegade American," had been "at the head of the murder." They tried to lynch him and "the strikers in his command," but Carmody had fortified his house, and a couple of hundred shots failed to dislodge him. No injuries or deaths from the exchange are reported.

A Socorro letter of September 28 reported that it was "now well understood" that Carmody had led the Wiggins mob, and that he was at Fort Craig under the protection of soldiers, which alone saved his life. The Herald's dispatch ended, "The end is not yet," but no report of an arrest, inquest or charge against either Carmody or his attackers was found.

The siege is known from a single Socorro dispatch printed in the Weekly Phoenix Herald on October 6 under the headline "Murdered," which was chiefly an attack on the Wiggins hanging as "an infamous outrage and cold blooded murder." That dispatch tied the killing to peonage in New Mexico and called Carmody "as big a rascal as ever went unhung," reporting the attempt on him without censure. The Albuquerque Morning Journal mentioned Carmody's flight to Fort Craig among routine Socorro news, while a Dakota regional brief reported only the Wiggins hanging.

The Dakota brief dated the Wiggins hanging to the 23d and blamed "a mob of Mexicans" with an unnamed instigator in old San Marcial, whereas both Socorro reports placed it on Friday and named Carmody as the suspected leader.

bases: A Socorro dispatch reports an attempt by a number of people to lynch Carmody and his men, besieging his fortified house with gunfire (A4); no one is reported killed.
A group of people tried to lynch Carmody without authority for his suspected leadership of the Wiggins hanging, but he held his house and no death is reported (A4); it was an attempted lynching.
Only the Phoenix Herald's Socorro dispatch describes the siege (A4); the Albuquerque letter supports the suspicion against Carmody and his need for protection but not the attack itself (A1).

accounts.label: Socorro dispatch (Phoenix Herald)
accounts.gist: After the Wiggins hanging, people concluded Carmody had led it and tried to lynch him and his men; he held his fortified house through some two hundred shots.

accounts.label: Socorro letter (Albuquerque Morning Journal)
accounts.gist: Carmody was understood to have led the mob that killed Wiggins and was at Fort Craig under soldiers' protection, which alone saved him.

accounts.label: Regional brief (Press and Daily Dakotaian)
accounts.gist: A mob of Mexicans hanged Wiggin on the 23d; no clue to the perpetrators, but a man in old San Marcial was supposed to be the instigator.

framing.detail: The Herald's dispatch condemned the Wiggins hanging as 'an infamous outrage and cold blooded murder' but reported the attempt on Carmody without censure, calling him a 'renegade American'.
The Albuquerque letter reported Carmody's protection at Fort Craig among local news items, praising Wiggins's military service.
